I pushed through for way longer than I should have. Tried a probiotic on its own, didn't touch the fog or the energy. Tried a multivitamin, made the nausea worse if I took it without eating properly, which on the jabs is most days.

What actually turned it around was Cloud. Three gummies, once a day, no tablets to choke down on a bad stomach morning. They have 36 superfood ingredients designed specifically for people on the jabs. Pat Greene was supposed to direct the choir at our church's hundredth anniversary celebration in October.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Two news crews from Channel 11 and Channel 5.

Pat sat in the back pew of the church she has served for twenty-two years, behind the third pillar on the left side where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to her twenty-eight-year-old assistant Roxanne Holcomb conduct her choir.

Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

I'm going to say something most of us on these GLP-1 medications do not want to hear, and I'm not going to soften it because Pat did not get a soft version of this either.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

My name is Gloria Mason. I'm 67. I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. By June of last year I weighed two hundred and thirty-four — the most I had ever weighed in my life. My doctor told me my blood pressure was a hundred and sixty over a hundred and that we had two paths in front of us. I chose Ozempic®.

I started in July. By December I was down to one eighty-six. My pressure was normal. I had started walking on the trail at Stone Mountain Park three mornings a week. I had bought a dress at Phipps Plaza I had not had the courage to try on in twelve years.

I should have been thanking the Lord. The woman in the photograph on my dresser and the woman in my mirror were starting to match again.

Instead, I was sixty-seven years old, sitting in the back pew at Sunday morning service holding a folded handkerchief over my mouth because I had not gone normally in nine days and I could feel a sulphur burp coming up.

The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

I tried what he said. I tried what Sister Carolyn from the Mothers Board suggested. I tried what my daughter Tracey saw on TikTok. By August I had been to the bathroom five times in three weeks.

I am a retired guidance counselor. I track things. Between February and August I spent five hundred and twenty dollars on supplements and laxatives. Miralax morning and night. Citrucel at lunch. Metamucil at dinner. A magnesium from the GNC at Camp Creek. A probiotic my daughter Tracey ordered from Amazon for forty-eight dollars. A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Patricia Anne Greene and I have been friends since 1968. We were both twelve years old, both in Sister Mae Hudson's youth choir at Greater Mt. Zion, both not very good singers if I am being honest with you. Pat had a voice like clear water by the time she was sixteen. I had a voice that does not need to be discussed further. Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt. Zion for twenty-two years.

Our congregation does not have a Sunday service without Pat at that piano. Pat has not had a Sunday morning without our congregation since 1985. Marcus called her the heartbeat of our church right up until the day he passed.

She started Mounjaro® a year before I started Ozempic — same kind of grief story, different husband, hers passed in 2021. She lost fifty-one pounds. By December of '24 she was running again — she had been a sprinter at Spelman, I do not know if I told you that — and she was three months into rehearsals for the church's hundredth anniversary celebration scheduled for October. The committee had been planning it for two years. Pat was going to direct twelve special selections, a full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta, three guest soloists, and a praise dance from the youth ministry. Bishop Brown was coming from Washington. Two news crews.

In February she had a constipation streak that went fourteen days. She did not tell me. She did not tell her son Marcus Junior up in Athens. She filled out her own discontinuation paperwork on a Saturday night when she was alone in her kitchen. She quit her shots that week.

By May she had gained back twenty-three pounds. By July she had stopped coming to choir rehearsal — sent Roxanne in her place. By September she was up forty-six pounds. The depression came in heavy by the third week of September. She missed three Sundays in a row. People were calling me asking if Pat was all right. I did not know what to say.

The hundredth anniversary celebration was Sunday morning, October the twenty-first. The sanctuary was full. The Bishop preached for fifty-two minutes. Roxanne stood at Pat's piano and conducted Pat's program. Roxanne is twenty-eight years old. She is a very gifted young woman, the granddaughter of one of Pat's choir mothers from the eighties. She did her best.

Pat sat in the back pew on the left side, behind the third pillar where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to twenty-two years of her work being conducted by a young woman who had not yet been born when Pat first sat down at that piano.

After the service I went looking for her. Her car was already gone.

The next morning the church board met. By Wednesday word had spread that they were discussing transitioning Pat to "Music Minister Emeritus" — a respectful title for a forced retirement none of us thought we would see. Roxanne would take over permanently in January.

I drove home from running errands on Tuesday afternoon and sat in my car in my own driveway for thirty-five minutes before I could go inside. I called my prescriber's office and scheduled the discontinuation appointment for Friday at one. I did not tell my daughters. I did not tell anyone.

The next Wednesday was my regular Bible study night at the church. Wednesday evening women's Bible study, six-thirty to eight, the same group of women I have been studying scripture with for sixteen years. I had not been the last four Wednesdays. I had been telling myself I would skip another one and stay home in front of the television.

I do not skip Bible study. I made myself go.

After the lesson ended at eight, the women's group cleaned up together — folding chairs, clearing coffee cups from the church's silver urns, wiping down the folding tables in the fellowship hall. There were six of us at the start of the cleanup. Most of the others had already gone home by the time I was folding the last three chairs.

Doreen Williams came back from the kitchen with a trash bag in her hand.

Doreen is seventy-two. She is one of the matriarchs of our church and a fellow Mothers Board member. She was the lead pharmacist at the Greene Brothers Pharmacy on Cascade Road in southwest Atlanta from 1981 until they closed in 2019 — thirty-eight years filling prescriptions for half the Black families on the southside of this city. She was Marcus's friend before she was mine. She and her husband John were at his funeral.

She set the trash bag down. She looked at me across the folding table.

"Gloria. Sister. You sit down. We need to talk before you drive yourself home."

I sat down.

I told her everything in about twelve minutes. The constipation. The burps in the receiving line. Pat. The discontinuation appointment Friday at one. I cried in the fellowship hall of the church Marcus and I had served for thirty-six years for the first time since the morning he passed.

Doreen handed me a clean napkin with the church's name printed at the corner from the stack on the table. Then she sat down across from me and folded her hands the way she used to do when she was about to explain to me what a new prescription would do to my husband's pressure.

"Sister Gloria. Can I tell you what I learned in thirty-eight years filling prescriptions at Greene Brothers?"

"Please."

"These medications — Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro — slow your gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That is how they make you feel full. That is how you got down to one eighty-six."

"I know that part."

"But here is what your prescriber did not tell you. When your stomach empties at half-speed, two things happen they do not put on the patient handout. First, food sits in your stomach long enough to ferment. Bacteria break down food that should have moved on six hours ago. That is where the sulphur burps come from. Second, the slowdown runs all the way through your gut. Stool sits longer. Dries. Compacts. By the time it reaches your colon, the muscle contractions your body normally uses to push it out are not strong enough to compensate."

"That is the constipation."

Losing the weight on a GLP-1 feels like a miracle, until the constipation hits and you realize why people actually quit.

I almost quit, too. I came within one click of giving up the only thing that had finally worked for me. What stopped me was finding out what was actually causing this, and that it could be fixed. Let me back up.

I started Wegovy® in February.

By April, I had lost twenty-four pounds. My clothes fit differently. My face looked different. People at work were starting to notice, and for the first time in my adult life, the food noise was just gone. I wasn't thinking about what I was going to eat next. I wasn't bargaining with myself at 9 PM. I was just living.

Nobody warned me about what was quietly happening in the background.

By week three, my bathroom trips had started spacing out. Every three days. Then every four. By month two, I was going every five or six days, and only with serious effort.

I started tracking it on my phone calendar. Just a small dot on the days it happened.

By March, there were very few dots.

I was terrified to eat. I remember sitting at my kitchen table one morning, staring at a piece of dry toast, feeling like my dinner from the night before was still sitting right at the top of my stomach. Like there was no room for anything new.

Day three without going was uncomfortable. Day four meant I was skipping lunch because the thought of adding anything else made me feel sick. Day five meant I was canceling plans and staying close to home, just in case something finally happened.

When I finally did go, it felt like I was passing stones. My entire abdomen ached. I would sit on the bathroom floor afterward, exhausted, wondering how I was supposed to keep doing this.

I called my prescriber in tears.

"Drink a gallon of water a day," she said. "Add more fiber. Take Miralax. Maybe add some psyllium husk at bedtime."

I did all of it.

I bought the orange tubs of Metamucil. I bought the blue bottles of Miralax. I drank so much water I felt like I was sloshing when I walked. I forced myself to eat broccoli and beans even though the thought of food made me gag.

I tried a probiotic gummy from the wellness aisle. I tried a magnesium citrate bottle from the pharmacy. I tried drinking warm lemon water first thing every morning because someone in a Facebook group swore by it.

By May, I had a wicker basket on my kitchen counter overflowing with bottles and tubs and packets. I added it up one night. Almost three hundred dollars, on things that had not worked.

I was still backed up for days at a time.

And the extra fiber was actually making the bloating worse. My stomach was so distended some evenings that I couldn't button my jeans. I looked like I was retaining everything I had ever eaten.

The fiber was supposed to be the fix. The fact that it was making things worse should have been a clue. I just didn't know what it was pointing to yet.

Still, I kept telling myself I just needed more time. That my body was still adjusting. That the next thing would be the one that finally worked. That is what I told myself for three months.

Dana and I had started our shots within a few weeks of each other. She was on Mounjaro®. I was on Wegovy®. We texted almost every day about it, the wins and the side effects both. She had lost twenty-two pounds by the time I had lost twenty-four. We were both thrilled.

By October, she had gained back twenty-seven.

She was back to where she had started, except now she also knew exactly what she had lost: the food noise finally quiet, her body finally working with her instead of against her.

"I just wish I had figured out the side effects," she said. "I would have stayed on it forever."

She never found her way out. I didn't know it sitting there across the table from her, but I was about to find the answer she never did.

I drove home thinking about Dana the entire way. The same basket on my counter. The same blank calendar. And I was starting to wonder if I was headed exactly where she was.

I pulled up my discontinuation paperwork that night and sat there a long time, looking at it.

I kept thinking about something I had read. That roughly 80% of people who stop a GLP-1 regain all the weight they lost within a year and a half. I did not want to be another line in that statistic. I had just watched it happen to Dana.

Twenty-four pounds gone. The food noise finally quiet.

"You don't need more bulk," she said. "You need to restore the movement signals. And you need to draw water gently back into the bowel so things can actually pass."

Daily, targeted, gentle support. Paired with a probiotic blend of the right species to help rebalance the gut environment and promote regularity from the inside.

"That combination is the main engine," she said. "The magnesium creates the conditions for movement. The probiotics help your gut remember how to move on its own."

The second layer was digestive support. Ginger root extract and peppermint to help calm the stomach and promote digestion while food is sitting longer than it should. Not ginger ale, which has almost no real ginger in it. A real extract, at a real dose.

And the third layer was nutritional support. Because on a GLP-1, you are eating a fraction of what you used to eat. Your body is not getting the vitamins and minerals it needs to keep everything running. That matters for your gut, your energy, your hair, your immune system. The whole engine needs fuel.

"But you cannot just buy random bottles off Amazon and expect them to work together," she said. "The doses have to be right, the forms have to be absorbable, and they have to be taken as one system instead of separately at random times. You need a formula that was actually designed for this specific situation, where everything is calibrated to work together."

By the time she finished, I had my list. The right forms, the right doses, the right species, all built to work together as one system, by someone who had actually studied what a GLP-1 does to your gut. I had spent months buying single bottles off a shelf. Not one of them checked more than one box.

She wrote down a name on a notepad and slid it across the desk.

Sylven.

The team at Sylven didn't start with a list of trending supplements and work backward. They started with the physiology. They spent months studying exactly what happens to the gut on a GLP-1 medication, what the slowed transit actually does to the microbiome, what forms of magnesium are absorbed at the right rate for daily use, which probiotic species have the most evidence for regularity support, and how the digestive enzyme blend needed to be structured to help break down food sitting in a slowed stomach.

Then they tested it.

Each round adjusted the doses, changed the forms, and tested how the ingredients behaved together as a system instead of a pile of separate pills, until it was dialed in.

The goal was not to create another GLP-1 supplement. The goal was to create the natural formulation that works *with* the way a GLP-1 changes your body, not against it.

Last March I found Wegovy® in my sister's bathroom cabinet.

I closed the door the way you'd close it if you'd just opened a letter that wasn't addressed to you. Quiet. Careful. Like I needed time to decide what I'd just seen.

Seeing a weight-loss drug behind her cotton pads felt like being lied to. A small confounding betrayal I'd needed her to be above.

I didn't speak to her for six months.

I'm on the same drug now.

And there's something I need to tell her before the symptom she's been hiding from me gets worse. I think it's already worse.

Let me back up.

My sister is forty-eight. I'm fifty-nine. We've been close in the way only sisters who survived the same childhood can be close. Three kids between us. One divorce survived (mine). Twenty-six years of Sunday dinners at our mother's table before our mother passed in 2022, and another three years of holding the family together at my kitchen table since.

She lives twelve miles from me in Eagle, Idaho. I live in Boise. I see her almost every week. Or I did, until that Saturday.

I was at her house helping wrap her daughter Maddie's tenth birthday gifts. We'd done this every year together since Maddie was born. She needed paper tape. She said it was in the bathroom drawer.

Behind a stack of cotton pads, in a folded CVS prescription bag, the Wegovy® label was visible through the plastic.

I stood there holding that drawer open for a long time. Then I closed it. I wrapped the gifts. I drank the coffee. I left two hours later without mentioning it.

I drove home and I told my husband Mike. Loudly. I told him she'd taken the easy way. I told him our mother would have been disappointed. I told him I thought she was stronger than that. I said the things you say at the kitchen counter when you're trying to make yourself feel better about a judgment you've just passed.

That night I didn't text her. She didn't text me.

Six months is a long time to not speak to your sister.

In April I missed my niece's birthday party. I lied to Mike about a migraine and stayed home.

In May our grandkids were on the same Little League team and I made sure I arrived after the first inning so we'd be sitting on opposite sides of the field.

In June I drafted a text four times and deleted it four times.

In July I unfollowed her on Instagram so I'd stop checking it.

In August I checked it anyway, on Mike's phone, while he was in the shower.

She'd lost more weight.

I ate the feeling for the rest of the month and into September.

In September my endocrinologist told me my A1C had climbed to 6.4.

She said, in plain English, that I was a year from an insulin pump if nothing changed.

She reminded me my mother had gone the insulin route at 52, and that I was already seven years past that.

She said the word Ozempic. She said Wegovy.

She said: "You have options your mother didn't have."

I drove home and I sat in the driveway for forty-five minutes before I went inside.

I thought about my sister.

I thought about what I'd said about her in my own kitchen seven months earlier.

I thought about my face in the bathroom mirror that night, saying "the real way."

I filled the Wegovy® prescription on a Monday.

I hid it in the glove compartment of my car until the Idaho afternoon sun moved off the windshield, because I didn't want it warming up in there. Then I brought it inside and put it in the back of the fridge.

I put it behind a jar of pickles Mike would never touch.

Then I stood in front of the open refrigerator for a long time looking at the pickle jar.

I had become the exact thing I had walked out of her bathroom for.

Same drug. Same shelf. Same jar.

I closed the fridge.

I lost 51 pounds in the next eight months.

I didn't tell anyone. Not Mike. Not my daughter Jenny in Portland. Not my son Tyler who lives ten minutes away. Especially not Diane.

I was coasting on the lie for a while.

I could take the drug and not have the conversation.

I could be a hypocrite in private.

Then at month three, I went six days without going to the bathroom.

Not painful at first. Just a slow, building bloat. I bought a tub of Metamucil at Albertsons and put it on the counter so Mike would think I was just being responsible about fiber.

Then the burps started.

You know the ones. The rotten-egg taste at the back of your throat. The kind that make the woman next to you on the elliptical at Boise Athletic Club move two machines down.

I cancelled book club. I cancelled lunch with my friend Karen. I told them I had a sinus thing.

By the end of month four I was waking up at three in the morning every single night.

I never told Mike.

Because the day I told him out loud was the day I'd have to choose between the drug that was finally getting my A1C in range and admitting I'd hidden it from him for ten months.

She ran a panel. Iron, ferritin, magnesium, thyroid, B12, protein.

Everything came back normal.

"This is just how some people respond to rapid weight loss," she said. "Increase your fiber. Add a daily Miralax. Take a magnesium tablet at bedtime if it gets bad. It's going to settle. Give it three to six months."

I did exactly what she said.

Week 1-4: Metamucil twice a day. Choked down the wet cardboard. Result: marginal first week, plateau.

Week 5-8: Switched to Miralax every morning. Result: 30% better, then back to baseline.

Week 9-12: My GP wrote me a prescription for Citrucel. $94 for a 60-day supply.

No different than Miralax. I was now spending $94 every two months on what was essentially expensive fiber.

Week 13-16: Amazon "GLP-1 multivitamin" that promised "complete gut support." $42 with overnight Prime.

Marginal first week. Plateau by week three.

I spent over $360 in four months on supplements and prescription fiber and stomach acid blockers because the Tylenol I was taking every night had burned a hole in my stomach lining.

I still hadn't gone normally in five months.

And I was starting to notice something else.

Sometimes at the top of the stairs I'd feel a little flutter in my chest. Not pain. Not enough to mention. Just enough to make me stop and put my hand on the bannister for a second before I kept going.

I told myself it was the stairs. I was 59. The stairs were going to get harder.

Then my friend Karen called me in February and told me her sister-in-law's cardiologist had found atrial fibrillation in a woman who'd lost 60 pounds on Mounjaro® in nine months.

"Karen," I said. "What does atrial fibrillation feel like?"

"Sometimes nothing," she said. "Sometimes a little flutter in your chest at the top of the stairs."

I sat down on my couch and didn't say anything for a long time.

The next morning I made an appointment with my GP for a referral.

Six-week wait for cardiology.

While I waited, I went to refill my Wegovy® at the independent pharmacy on Bannock Street in downtown Boise. Coleman Pharmacy. I'd been going there for four years — small, two-pharmacist shop, owned by a woman named Dr. Sarah Coleman who'd been a hospital pharmacist at St. Luke's Boise for thirty-one years before opening her own place.

She knew my whole medication history. She knew my A1C numbers. She knew my mother had been her patient at St. Luke's.

When she handed me my prescription, she asked the question my GP never asked.

"How are you actually feeling, Carol?"

I told her. The bowel movements. The burps. The Tylenol. The Amazon multivitamin. The fluttering at the top of the stairs.

She set the prescription bag down very slowly on the counter and looked at me.

"Carol. Come to the back."

She walked me to a small consultation room where she did her medication-therapy reviews. Sat me down at a table. Then she opened a binder and turned to a page near the front.

"Can I tell you something I learned in thirty-one years filling prescriptions for every medication you can name?"

I nodded.

"Your GP told you the truth about your symptoms. But she told you only half of it. There's not one problem happening here. There are two. And almost no GP is addressing the second one because it doesn't show up in standard labs."

She slid the binder across the table to me.

"Your medication — Wegovy®, Ozempic®, Mounjaro® — they slow gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That's the therapeutic effect. It's why your A1C dropped. It's also why food sits in your stomach long enough to start fermenting. Those are the sulfur burps. And it's why your intestinal motility slowed, which is the constipation. Your GP is treating those symptoms. She's not wrong about them. They're real, and with the right protocol they resolve."

"Okay."

"But here's what almost nobody is telling women on GLP-1s. While you've been losing weight, your body has been depleting its magnesium stores at three times the normal rate. Rapid fat loss triggers it. Reduced food intake compounds it. And the magnesium that goes first is the magnesium your body considers most disposable — which is not, unfortunately, the magnesium in your blood. It's the magnesium in your tissues. Your cardiac muscle. Your nerve endings. Your bone."

"But my magnesium test was normal."

"Carol. Less than one percent of your body's magnesium is in your blood. The blood test tells you what's in the bloodstream right now. It tells you almost nothing about what's in your heart muscle. Or your nerves. Or your bones. The body protects serum magnesium last and hardest, because if blood magnesium crashes, you die. So it strips the tissues first. The blood looks fine for months while the tissues quietly empty out."

I thought about the flutter at the top of the stairs.

She kept going.

"Magnesium is the cofactor for over six hundred enzymatic processes in your body. The two most magnesium-dependent tissues you have are your cardiac muscle and your neural tissue. When you deplete tissue magnesium fast — and a GLP-1 patient losing weight is depleting it fast — the cardiac muscle starts having trouble relaxing properly between contractions. That's how atrial fibrillation begins. Quietly. Intermittently. Before anyone catches it on an EKG."

"That's what's happening when I feel the flutter."

"I would bet on it. And here's the worst part. The fiber and the Miralax your GP gave you — those don't address it. The Amazon multivitamin you tried — that doesn't address it either. Most generic magnesium tablets are magnesium oxide, which your gut barely absorbs. The magnesium that actually reaches the tissue has to be a bioavailable form — citrate, glycinate, or a combination — at a therapeutic dose, paired with something that addresses the gastric emptying side."

"Why has nobody told me this?"

"Because the supplement industry has spent thirty years selling fiber to constipated people. The GLP-1 wave is brand new. Ninety percent of what's on Amazon under that label is under-dosed magnesium with no real ginger and no thought to the actual mechanism."

She turned the page in the binder.

"Brand B — labeled 200mg ginger root extract — was unstandardized commercial powder. No measurable gingerols. Useless."

"Brand C — labeled 500mg magnesium citrate — was magnesium oxide, which your body absorbs maybe 4% of."

"Brand D was contaminated with heavy metals at levels above the FDA's CFR-111 limits."

She paused.

"Exactly one product passed the assay. Magnesium delivered as labeled, in bioavailable citrate-glycinate form. Ginger root standardized to 5% gingerols. Methylcobalamin B12, not the cheap cyanocobalamin synthetic. Manufactured in a single FDA-registered facility in Ruston, Utah. Third-party tested every batch. No fillers."

She wrote a name on the back of a prescription pad.

"GLP-1 SOS™. Started by a woman who was on Wegovy® and went through what you're going through. She found a formulator who actually understood the dual mechanism. I recommend it to every GLP-1 patient who walks into this pharmacy now. I have no business relationship with the company. I just don't want to keep watching women like you end up in cardiology waiting rooms for something that was preventable."

I looked at the prescription pad. GLP-1 SOS™.

"And this fixes both problems?"

"If you start now, before the cardiac symptoms become a confirmed diagnosis — yes. Two capsules with dinner. Magnesium pulls water into your gut gently overnight and reaches the depleted tissue including the cardiac muscle. Ginger speeds gastric emptying enough to stop the fermentation. B12 rebuilds the nerve and energy reserves. You should see regularity in three days. Sulfur burps usually resolve in 48 hours. The fluttering — if it really is early magnesium depletion — should settle within four to six weeks as the tissue stores rebuild."

"What about my cardiology appointment?"

"Keep it. Tell the cardiologist exactly what we just discussed. Ask her about intracellular magnesium testing if she's seeing rhythm signals. But start the supplement tonight, not after the appointment. Every week you wait is a week the tissue keeps depleting."

"How much is it?"

"$24.99 a month on subscription. Less than what you're already spending on Citrucel and Tylenol and the stomach acid blocker for the lining damage the Tylenol caused. And it has a 60-day money-back guarantee. If it doesn't work for you, you get every dollar back, no return required."

I ordered it from the parking lot.

Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. I started to wonder if Dr. Coleman was wrong.

Day three, I went. Gently. No cramping. No urgency. Just normal. I sat on the edge of the tub afterward for a minute because I'd forgotten what normal felt like.

✅ 48 hours after my first dose: I had coffee with Karen at our usual spot. I waited for the sulfur burps. They didn't come.

✅ Week 2: I slept through the night without cramping. Eight hours straight for the first time since September.

✅ Week 3: I had energy at 3 PM. I weeded the entire front yard. I hadn't done that since the spring.

✅ Week 4: Mike and I went out for our anniversary at Chandlers downtown and I sat for two and a half hours and ate prime rib and never once thought about the bathroom.

✅ Week 5: I climbed the stairs at home and at the top, I waited. The flutter didn't come.

✅ Week 8: My A1C check came back at 5.7. Not 6.4. Not 5.9. Five point seven. My endocrinologist asked what I'd changed. I told her. She wrote it down.

Then I went to my cardiology appointment.

Saint Alphonsus on West Emerald.

I'd been doing fine for six weeks but I kept the appointment because Dr. Coleman had said to.

The cardiology waiting room is on the second floor. Soft fluorescent lighting. Vinyl chairs. People magazine. Botanical prints on the walls. I checked in and sat down with a clipboard.

Four chairs to my left, on the opposite side of the same row, was my sister.

Diane.

She was wearing an oversized cream cardigan that hung off her shoulders. She'd lost more weight since August — I could see it now even through the sweater. Her hair was in a low loose ponytail. She had a glucose monitor in her open canvas tote on the chair beside her, showing a reading I couldn't make out.

The cardigan was hiding loose skin under her arms. I knew that cardigan. She'd bought it the year our mother died because she needed something soft to wear to the visitation. She'd worn it almost every day for a month after.

She didn't see me.

I sat there with my clipboard in my lap for a long time without filling it out. I watched her.

She was staring at her hands.

She had her right hand pressed lightly against her sternum, the way you do when you're not in pain but you're waiting for the not-pain to turn into pain.

I knew that gesture. I'd been doing it on the stairs for five months.

Diane had been doing it longer.

She hadn't told me. We hadn't been speaking.

She hadn't told anyone, I would guess. Her husband John. Her son Tyler in college. Nobody.

Because the day she said it out loud was the day she'd have to admit, to the people she loved, that the drug she'd been hiding behind cotton pads was the same drug that had brought her to a cardiology waiting room on a Tuesday in February.

I sat there.

I almost got up. I almost crossed the four chairs. I almost said her name.

Then the receptionist called me. "Carol Hendricks?"

I stood up. I picked up my clipboard. I walked past her row. She still didn't look up.

I went into my appointment.

The cardiologist examined me, listened to my heart for a long time, ran the EKG. Then she sat across from me at her little desk and said: "Whatever you're doing, keep doing it. Your rhythm is fine. You're going to be fine."

I asked her about intracellular magnesium testing. She looked at me strangely and said it wasn't standard. But she said she had been seeing a noticeable uptick in rhythm complaints from GLP-1 patients in the last eight months and that if I was being proactive about it, I was probably saving her a future appointment.

I left her office. I walked back through the waiting room.

The chair where Diane had been sitting was empty.

I drove home, opened my laptop, and started writing.

If you're on a GLP-1 medication, or you're about to start one, or you're five months in and you're starting to feel a flutter at the top of the stairs, please understand what I didn't understand until a pharmacist drew me a diagram on the back of a prescription pad.

You're skipping your grandson's first birthday because the cramping has been worse this week and you don't want to ruin the day.

You're hiding the Wegovy® behind the pickles because the day you admit you're still on it is the day Mike will ask why you haven't gotten off it yet, which is the question you don't have an answer to.

You're sitting in a cardiology waiting room four chairs away from your sister and neither of you is looking at the other.

You don't want that. I didn't want that.

content.body:
Pat Greene was supposed to direct the choir at our church's hundredth anniversary celebration in October.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Two news crews from Channel 11 and Channel 5.

Pat sat in the back pew of the church she has served for twenty-two years, behind the third pillar on the left side where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to her twenty-eight-year-old assistant Roxanne Holcomb conduct her choir.

Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

I'm going to say something most of us on these GLP-1 medications do not want to hear, and I'm not going to soften it because Pat did not get a soft version of this either.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

My name is Gloria Mason. I'm 67. I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. By June of last year I weighed two hundred and thirty-four — the most I had ever weighed in my life. My doctor told me my blood pressure was a hundred and sixty over a hundred and that we had two paths in front of us. I chose Ozempic®.

I started in July. By December I was down to one eighty-six. My pressure was normal. I had started walking on the trail at Stone Mountain Park three mornings a week. I had bought a dress at Phipps Plaza I had not had the courage to try on in twelve years.

I should have been thanking the Lord. The woman in the photograph on my dresser and the woman in my mirror were starting to match again.

Instead, I was sixty-seven years old, sitting in the back pew at Sunday morning service holding a folded handkerchief over my mouth because I had not gone normally in nine days and I could feel a sulphur burp coming up.

The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

I tried what he said. I tried what Sister Carolyn from the Mothers Board suggested. I tried what my daughter Tracey saw on TikTok. By August I had been to the bathroom five times in three weeks.

I am a retired guidance counselor. I track things. Between February and August I spent five hundred and twenty dollars on supplements and laxatives. Miralax morning and night. Citrucel at lunch. Metamucil at dinner. A magnesium from the GNC at Camp Creek. A probiotic my daughter Tracey ordered from Amazon for forty-eight dollars. A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Patricia Anne Greene and I have been friends since 1968. We were both twelve years old, both in Sister Mae Hudson's youth choir at Greater Mt. Zion, both not very good singers if I am being honest with you. Pat had a voice like clear water by the time she was sixteen. I had a voice that does not need to be discussed further. Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt. Zion for twenty-two years.

Our congregation does not have a Sunday service without Pat at that piano. Pat has not had a Sunday morning without our congregation since 1985. Marcus called her the heartbeat of our church right up until the day he passed.

She started Mounjaro® a year before I started Ozempic — same kind of grief story, different husband, hers passed in 2021. She lost fifty-one pounds. By December of '24 she was running again — she had been a sprinter at Spelman, I do not know if I told you that — and she was three months into rehearsals for the church's hundredth anniversary celebration scheduled for October. The committee had been planning it for two years. Pat was going to direct twelve special selections, a full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta, three guest soloists, and a praise dance from the youth ministry. Bishop Brown was coming from Washington. Two news crews.

In February she had a constipation streak that went fourteen days. She did not tell me. She did not tell her son Marcus Junior up in Athens. She filled out her own discontinuation paperwork on a Saturday night when she was alone in her kitchen. She quit her shots that week.

By May she had gained back twenty-three pounds. By July she had stopped coming to choir rehearsal — sent Roxanne in her place. By September she was up forty-six pounds. The depression came in heavy by the third week of September. She missed three Sundays in a row. People were calling me asking if Pat was all right. I did not know what to say.

The hundredth anniversary celebration was Sunday morning, October the twenty-first. The sanctuary was full. The Bishop preached for fifty-two minutes. Roxanne stood at Pat's piano and conducted Pat's program. Roxanne is twenty-eight years old. She is a very gifted young woman, the granddaughter of one of Pat's choir mothers from the eighties. She did her best.

Pat sat in the back pew on the left side, behind the third pillar where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to twenty-two years of her work being conducted by a young woman who had not yet been born when Pat first sat down at that piano.

After the service I went looking for her. Her car was already gone.

The next morning the church board met. By Wednesday word had spread that they were discussing transitioning Pat to "Music Minister Emeritus" — a respectful title for a forced retirement none of us thought we would see. Roxanne would take over permanently in January.

I drove home from running errands on Tuesday afternoon and sat in my car in my own driveway for thirty-five minutes before I could go inside. I called my prescriber's office and scheduled the discontinuation appointment for Friday at one. I did not tell my daughters. I did not tell anyone.

The next Wednesday was my regular Bible study night at the church. Wednesday evening women's Bible study, six-thirty to eight, the same group of women I have been studying scripture with for sixteen years. I had not been the last four Wednesdays. I had been telling myself I would skip another one and stay home in front of the television.

I do not skip Bible study. I made myself go.

After the lesson ended at eight, the women's group cleaned up together — folding chairs, clearing coffee cups from the church's silver urns, wiping down the folding tables in the fellowship hall. There were six of us at the start of the cleanup. Most of the others had already gone home by the time I was folding the last three chairs.

Doreen Williams came back from the kitchen with a trash bag in her hand.

Doreen is seventy-two. She is one of the matriarchs of our church and a fellow Mothers Board member. She was the lead pharmacist at the Greene Brothers Pharmacy on Cascade Road in southwest Atlanta from 1981 until they closed in 2019 — thirty-eight years filling prescriptions for half the Black families on the southside of this city. She was Marcus's friend before she was mine. She and her husband John were at his funeral.

She set the trash bag down. She looked at me across the folding table.

"Gloria. Sister. You sit down. We need to talk before you drive yourself home."

I sat down.

I told her everything in about twelve minutes. The constipation. The burps in the receiving line. Pat. The discontinuation appointment Friday at one. I cried in the fellowship hall of the church Marcus and I had served for thirty-six years for the first time since the morning he passed.

Doreen handed me a clean napkin with the church's name printed at the corner from the stack on the table. Then she sat down across from me and folded her hands the way she used to do when she was about to explain to me what a new prescription would do to my husband's pressure.

"Sister Gloria. Can I tell you what I learned in thirty-eight years filling prescriptions at Greene Brothers?"

"Please."

"These medications — Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro — slow your gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That is how they make you feel full. That is how you got down to one eighty-six."

"I know that part."

"But here is what your prescriber did not tell you. When your stomach empties at half-speed, two things happen they do not put on the patient handout. First, food sits in your stomach long enough to ferment. Bacteria break down food that should have moved on six hours ago. That is where the sulphur burps come from. Second, the slowdown runs all the way through your gut. Stool sits longer. Dries. Compacts. By the time it reaches your colon, the muscle contractions your body normally uses to push it out are not strong enough to compensate."

"That is the constipation."

"That is the constipation. Now let me tell you what the supplement industry has been doing to women like us for the last two years."

"Tell me."

"Fiber works by adding bulk that needs gut motility — muscle contractions — to push it through. But your medication is intentionally suppressing those contractions. When you add fiber on a GLP-1, you are adding bulk that has nowhere to go. You are not relieving constipation. You are making the bloating worse."

I thought about every morning of forced Citrucel water I drank at the kitchen sink before I drove to Tuesday daycare at Kendra's.

"Stimulant laxatives — Dulcolax, Senna, Smooth Move — they force the intestinal muscles to contract. But your medication is suppressing those exact contractions. The two drugs fight each other inside your gut. The GLP-1 wins almost every time. That is why you have been cramping at three in the morning and still not going."

I thought about the night in August when I had taken three Senna tablets and missed the next morning's Mothers Board breakfast for the first time in nine years.

"What works?"

"You need an osmotic mechanism. Magnesium pulls water into your colon without requiring muscle contractions. That is the correct approach for a slowed system. But the dose has to be right, and most of what is on the shelf at the GNC or on Amazon is not the dose on the label."

"What else?"

"You need a prokinetic — something that speeds your gastric emptying enough to stop the fermentation, but does not fight the medication. There is exactly one botanical that does this reliably. Ginger root extract, at a specific dose and gingerol standardization. The supplement industry has been selling unstandardized ginger powder under premium labels for years. Most of it has no measurable active compound at all."

"How do you know?"

"My daughter Renee works at a contract testing lab in Norcross. She runs assays on commercial supplements when one company is suing another for label fraud. Last year she ran a panel on twelve GLP-1-positioned supplements being sold to women like you and me. Nine were underdosed on magnesium. Five had no measurable gingerols. Two contained heavy metals above CFR-111 limits. One was three percent of the magnesium it claimed on the label."

"How many passed?"

"One. Just one."

She wrote a name on the back of the Bible study handout, where the verse memorization section had been left blank.

"GLP-1 SOS™. Started by a woman who was on Wegovy and went through what you are going through. She found a real formulator and got it right. Losing the weight on a GLP-1 feels like a miracle, until the constipation hits and you realize why people actually quit.

I almost quit, too. I came within one click of giving up the only thing that had finally worked for me. What stopped me was finding out what was actually causing this, and that it could be fixed. Let me back up.

I started Wegovy® in February.

By April, I had lost twenty-four pounds. My clothes fit differently. My face looked different. People at work were starting to notice, and for the first time in my adult life, the food noise was just gone. I wasn't thinking about what I was going to eat next. By week three, my bathroom trips had started spacing out. Every three days. Then every four. By month two, I was going every five or six days, and only with serious effort.

I started tracking it on my phone calendar. Just a small dot on the days it happened.

By March, there were very few dots.

I was terrified to eat. I remember sitting at my kitchen table one morning, staring at a piece of dry toast, feeling like my dinner from the night before was still sitting right at the top of my stomach. Like there was no room for anything new.

Day three without going was uncomfortable. Day four meant I was skipping lunch because the thought of adding anything else made me feel sick. Day five meant I was canceling plans and staying close to home, just in case something finally happened.

When I finally did go, it felt like I was passing stones. My entire abdomen ached. I would sit on the bathroom floor afterward, exhausted, wondering how I was supposed to keep doing this.

I called my prescriber in tears.

"Drink a gallon of water a day," she said. "Add more fiber. Take Miralax. Maybe add some psyllium husk at bedtime."

I did all of it.

I bought the orange tubs of Metamucil. I bought the blue bottles of Miralax. I drank so much water I felt like I was sloshing when I walked. I forced myself to eat broccoli and beans even though the thought of food made me gag.

I tried a probiotic gummy from the wellness aisle. I tried a magnesium citrate bottle from the pharmacy. I tried drinking warm lemon water first thing every morning because someone in a Facebook group swore by it.

I was still backed up for days at a time.

And the extra fiber was actually making the bloating worse. My stomach was so distended some evenings that I couldn't button my jeans. I looked like I was retaining everything I had ever eaten.

The fiber was supposed to be the fix. The fact that it was making things worse should have been a clue. I just didn't know what it was pointing to yet.

Still, I kept telling myself I just needed more time. That my body was still adjusting. That the next thing would be the one that finally worked. That is what I told myself for three months.

And then I watched what happened to my friend Dana.

Dana and I had started our shots within a few weeks of each other. She was on Mounjaro®. I was on Wegovy®. We texted almost every day about it, the wins and the side effects both. She had lost twenty-two pounds by the time I had lost twenty-four. We were both thrilled.

She never found her way out. I didn't know it sitting there across the table from her, but I was about to find the answer she never did.

I drove home thinking about Dana the entire way. The same basket on my counter. The same blank calendar. And I was starting to wonder if I was headed exactly where she was.

I pulled up my discontinuation paperwork that night and sat there a long time, looking at it.

I kept thinking about something I had read. That roughly 80% of people who stop a GLP-1 regain all the weight they lost within a year and a half. I did not want to be another line in that statistic. I had just watched it happen to Dana.

Twenty-four pounds gone. The food noise finally quiet.

The second layer was digestive support. Ginger root extract and peppermint to help calm the stomach and promote digestion while food is sitting longer than it should. Not ginger ale, which has almost no real ginger in it. A real extract, at a real dose.

And the third layer was nutritional support. Because on a GLP-1, you are eating a fraction of what you used to eat. Your body is not getting the vitamins and minerals it needs to keep everything running. That matters for your gut, your energy, your hair, your immune system. The whole engine needs fuel.

"The doses have to be right, the forms have to be absorbable, and they have to be taken as one system instead of separately at random times. You need a formula that was actually designed for this specific situation, where everything is calibrated to work together."

By the time she finished, I had my list. I had spent months buying single bottles off a shelf. Not one of them checked more than one box.

Sylven.

Pat Greene was supposed to direct the choir at our church's hundredth anniversary celebration in October.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Two news crews from Channel 11 and Channel 5.

Pat sat in the back pew of the church she has served for twenty-two years, behind the third pillar on the left side where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to her twenty-eight-year-old assistant Roxanne Holcomb conduct her choir.

Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

I'm going to say something most of us on these GLP-1 medications do not want to hear, and I'm not going to soften it because Pat did not get a soft version of this either.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

My name is Gloria Mason. I'm 67. I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. By June of last year I weighed two hundred and thirty-four — the most I had ever weighed in my life. My doctor told me my blood pressure was a hundred and sixty over a hundred and that we had two paths in front of us. I chose Ozempic®.

I started in July. By December I was down to one eighty-six. My pressure was normal. I had started walking on the trail at Stone Mountain Park three mornings a week. I had bought a dress at Phipps Plaza I had not had the courage to try on in twelve years.

I should have been thanking the Lord. The woman in the photograph on my dresser and the woman in my mirror were starting to match again.

Instead, I was sixty-seven years old, sitting in the back pew at Sunday morning service holding a folded handkerchief over my mouth because I had not gone normally in nine days and I could feel a sulphur burp coming up.

The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

I tried what he said. I tried what Sister Carolyn from the Mothers Board suggested. I tried what my daughter Tracey saw on TikTok. By August I had been to the bathroom five times in three weeks.

I am a retired guidance counselor. I track things. Between February and August I spent five hundred and twenty dollars on supplements and laxatives. Miralax morning and night. Citrucel at lunch. Metamucil at dinner. A magnesium from the GNC at Camp Creek. A probiotic my daughter Tracey ordered from Amazon for forty-eight dollars. A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Patricia Anne Greene and I have been friends since 1968. We were both twelve years old, both in Sister Mae Hudson's youth choir at Greater Mt. Zion, both not very good singers if I am being honest with you. Pat had a voice like clear water by the time she was sixteen. I had a voice that does not need to be discussed further. Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt. Zion for twenty-two years.

Our congregation does not have a Sunday service without Pat at that piano. Pat has not had a Sunday morning without our congregation since 1985. Marcus called her the heartbeat of our church right up until the day he passed.

She started Mounjaro® a year before I started Ozempic — same kind of grief story, different husband, hers passed in 2021. She lost fifty-one pounds. By December of '24 she was running again — she had been a sprinter at Spelman, I do not know if I told you that — and she was three months into rehearsals for the church's hundredth anniversary celebration scheduled for October. The committee had been planning it for two years. Pat was going to direct twelve special selections, a full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta, three guest soloists, and a praise dance from the youth ministry. Bishop Brown was coming from Washington. Two news crews.

In February she had a constipation streak that went fourteen days. She did not tell me. She did not tell her son Marcus Junior up in Athens. She filled out her own discontinuation paperwork on a Saturday night when she was alone in her kitchen. She quit her shots that week.

By May she had gained back twenty-three pounds. By July she had stopped coming to choir rehearsal — sent Roxanne in her place. By September she was up forty-six pounds. The depression came in heavy by the third week of September. She missed three Sundays in a row. People were calling me asking if Pat was all right. I did not know what to say.

The hundredth anniversary celebration was Sunday morning, October the twenty-first. The sanctuary was full. The Bishop preached for fifty-two minutes. Roxanne stood at Pat's piano and conducted Pat's program. Roxanne is twenty-eight years old. She is a very gifted young woman, the granddaughter of one of Pat's choir mothers from the eighties. She did her best.

Pat sat in the back pew on the left side, behind the third pillar where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to twenty-two years of her work being conducted by a young woman who had not yet been born when Pat first sat down at that piano.

After the service I went looking for her. Her car was already gone.

The next morning the church board met. By Wednesday word had spread that they were discussing transitioning Pat to "Music Minister Emeritus" — a respectful title for a forced retirement none of us thought we would see. Roxanne would take over permanently in January.

I drove home from running errands on Tuesday afternoon and sat in my car in my own driveway for thirty-five minutes before I could go inside. I called my prescriber's office and scheduled the discontinuation appointment for Friday at one. I did not tell my daughters. I did not tell anyone.

The next Wednesday was my regular Bible study night at the church. Wednesday evening women's Bible study, six-thirty to eight, the same group of women I have been studying scripture with for sixteen years. I had not been the last four Wednesdays. I had been telling myself I would skip another one and stay home in front of the television.

I do not skip Bible study. I made myself go.

After the lesson ended at eight, the women's group cleaned up together — folding chairs, clearing coffee cups from the church's silver urns, wiping down the folding tables in the fellowship hall. There were six of us at the start of the cleanup. Most of the others had already gone home by the time I was folding the last three chairs.

Doreen Williams came back from the kitchen with a trash bag in her hand.

Doreen is seventy-two. She is one of the matriarchs of our church and a fellow Mothers Board member. She was the lead pharmacist at the Greene Brothers Pharmacy on Cascade Road in southwest Atlanta from 1981 until they closed in 2019 — thirty-eight years filling prescriptions for half the Black families on the southside of this city. She was Marcus's friend before she was mine. She and her husband John were at his funeral.

She set the trash bag down. She looked at me across the folding table.

"Gloria. Sister. You sit down. We need to talk before you drive yourself home."

I sat down.

I told her everything in about twelve minutes. The constipation. The burps in the receiving line. Pat. The discontinuation appointment Friday at one. I cried in the fellowship hall of the church Marcus and I had served for thirty-six years for the first time since the morning he passed.

Doreen handed me a clean napkin with the church's name printed at the corner from the stack on the table. Then she sat down across from me and folded her hands the way she used to do when she was about to explain to me what a new prescription would do to my husband's pressure.

"Sister Gloria. Can I tell you what I learned in thirty-eight years filling prescriptions at Greene Brothers?"

"Please."

"These medications — Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro — slow your gastric emptying by fifty percent or more. That is how they make you feel full. That is how you got down to one eighty-six."

"I know that part."

"But here is what your prescriber did not tell you. When your stomach empties at half-speed, two things happen they do not put on the patient handout. First, food sits in your stomach long enough to ferment. Bacteria break down food that should have moved on six hours ago. That is where the sulphur burps come from. Second, the slowdown runs all the way through your gut. Stool sits longer. Dries. Compacts. By the time it reaches your colon, the muscle contractions your body normally uses to push it out are not strong enough to compensate."

"That is the constipation."

"That is the constipation. Now let me tell you what the supplement industry has been doing to women like us for the last two years."

"Tell me."

"Fiber works by adding bulk that needs gut motility — muscle contractions — to push it through. But your medication is intentionally suppressing those contractions. When you add fiber on a GLP-1, you are adding bulk that has nowhere to go. You are not relieving constipation. You are making the bloating worse."

I thought about every morning of forced Citrucel water I drank at the kitchen sink before I drove to Tuesday daycare at Kendra's.

"Stimulant laxatives — Dulcolax, Senna, Smooth Move — they force the intestinal muscles to contract. But your medication is suppressing those exact contractions. The two drugs fight each other inside your gut. The GLP-1 wins almost every time. That is why you have been cramping at three in the morning and still not going."

I thought about the night in August when I had taken three Senna tablets and missed the next morning's Mothers Board breakfast for the first time in nine years.

"What works?"

"You need an osmotic mechanism. Magnesium pulls water into your colon without requiring muscle contractions. That is the correct approach for a slowed system. But the dose has to be right, and most of what is on the shelf at the GNC or on Amazon is not the dose on the label."

"What else?"

"You need a prokinetic — something that speeds your gastric emptying enough to stop the fermentation, but does not fight the medication. There is exactly one botanical that does this reliably. Ginger root extract, at a specific dose and gingerol standardization. The supplement industry has been selling unstandardized ginger powder under premium labels for years. Most of it has no measurable active compound at all."

"How do you know?"

"My daughter Renee works at a contract testing lab in Norcross. She runs assays on commercial supplements when one company is suing another for label fraud. Last year she ran a panel on twelve GLP-1-positioned supplements being sold to women like you and me. Nine were underdosed on magnesium. Five had no measurable gingerols. Two contained heavy metals above CFR-111 limits. One was three percent of the magnesium it claimed on the label."

"How many passed?"

"One. Just one."

She wrote a name on the back of the Bible study handout, where the verse memorization section had been left blank.

"GLP-1 SOS™. Started by a woman who was on Wegovy and went through what you are going through. She found a real formulator and got it right. I have told every Mother on this board who is on these medications. I have told the deaconess at Big Bethel. I have no business relationship with the company. I just do not want any more Pats."

I looked at the handout. GLP-1 SOS™ written in Doreen's careful pharmacist's print. Then I looked at her.

"Will this work for Pat?"

"It will work for Pat if she will take it. Right now, you. Two capsules with dinner. The magnesium pulls water in gently overnight. The ginger speeds your stomach emptying. Regularity inside three or four days. Sulphur burps usually gone within forty-eight hours. Energy back in the second or third week as the B12 builds up."

I cancelled the discontinuation appointment from the church parking lot before I drove home. I ordered GLP-1 SOS™ from glp1sos.com that night at the kitchen table where Marcus and I had taken every meal of our marriage.

Day one, nothing. Day two, nothing. Day three, I went, in my own bathroom, gently, at six fifty AM. No cramping. No straining. Just normal.

I sat on the edge of the tub for a minute afterward and let myself believe it.

Forty-eight hours after my first dose, I stood next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service and shook the hands of about a hundred and forty members of my congregation without covering my mouth with a handkerchief once.

Week two, I slept through the night for the first time since March.

Week three, I had energy at three in the afternoon for the first time since the spring.

Week four, I kept the grandbabies on a Tuesday and a Thursday and on Saturday I drove down to Athens for the afternoon to visit Kendra's mother-in-law at her assisted living facility. I did not fall asleep once.

I am still on Ozempic®. Down to one eighty-two. My blood pressure last visit was one twenty-eight over seventy-six. My doctor said it is the best she has seen on me in twenty years.

That was eight weeks ago. Haven't been constipated since. Haven't had a sulphur burp since.

Every time I see Pat — who is back on Mounjaro now and four weeks into her own bottle of GLP-1 SOS™ — I think about her sitting behind the third pillar. The church board has agreed to delay any Emeritus decision until February. Pat is going to direct the Christmas concert on December the fifteenth. Roxanne will play the offertory. They have already had three rehearsals.

I'm writing this because I keep seeing the same posts in the Black women's GLP-1 groups my daughter Tracey added me to.

"On Ozempic. Constipated ten days. Tried everything Sister Linda recommended on TikTok. Anyone?"

"Sulphur burps so bad I skipped Sunday service last week. Help."

"Twelve days. Considering quitting. Anybody got anything?"

You are not doing anything wrong. The fiber is not the problem. The brand is not the problem. The mechanism is the problem.
