"I've done everything the cortisol people told me to do. My hair is still falling out. My endo finally ran ferritin. It was 18. Why is the entire GLP-1 hair loss conversation about cortisol and not about iron?"

11:47pm. I open the patient portal again. 

"Iron: 87 mcg/dL. Normal"

Same as the last 2 weeks.

The number doesn't change.

I run my hand through my hair and three more strands come with it.

Four.

Six.

Twelve.

There friggin' everywhere. 

I literally can't keep counting or I'll go nuts.

========

I used to be the girl who had to thin out her ponytail because the elastic kept snapping.

The girl whose stylist sighed and said "we'll need an extra hour for the color, you have so much."

The girl in every wedding photo with the hair that made people lean in and ask.

The girl whose senior year photo my mother still keeps on the mantel because, in my mother's words, "that's the year your hair really came in."

That girl filled an exam room with shed strands and got told she was fine.

========

I started Tirz in March.

By August I'd lost 41 pounds.

I'd also lost what felt like half my hair.

I am not making this up.

The shower drain caught what looked like the tail of a small animal every week.

My pillow at 6am looked like I'd shared it with someone.

I emptied my brush three times getting ready, not once.

But here's the thing.

I did the responsible thing.

I asked.

I said the words out loud, sitting in her exam room.

"Could it be iron? My mom always had low iron. I haven't been able to eat red meat since I started the shot."

She nodded.

She ordered the test.

She called me a week later.

"Your iron's great. It's just the shot. Hair grows back. Probably stress."

I drove home thinking... well. At least I know.

For two weeks I felt vindicated.

For three months I watched my hair keep falling.

========

I tried everything that came up.

Biotin. Two bottles. $39.

The collagen everyone in the Facebook groups swears by. $94 a month for four months. $376 down the drain.

The hair vitamin you've seen advertised by 17 different influencers. Three months. $237.

Minoxidil foam from the dermatologist after I begged for an appointment. $84 and a hairline I had to baby for six weeks before I gave up.

Ferrous sulfate. Two bottles. $26. Constipated me for three months and my hair kept falling exactly the same way.

Liquid iron from the health food store, the kind that costs $58 and tastes like a penny dipped in molasses. Four months.

A scalp serum with copper peptides. $179.

Two rounds of PRP injections at my dermatologist's office. $1,100.

The math doesn't lie.

$2,141 in six months.

Zero hairs saved.

========

The friend who finally cracked it open for me was Liz.

We've known each other since freshman year of college and we still text every day.

Liz works in pharma sales.

Liz hears things at conferences that take three years to make it to anyone else.

Liz had also lost 30 pounds on Mounjaro the year before and we'd cried about her hair on FaceTime in April.

In October she texted me at 8pm on a Wednesday.

Just a phone number.

And then... "Call her. She's a nurse practitioner. Hematology and women's health. She's the one who fixed me."

I called the number on my lunch break the next day.

Her name was Renee.

Renee answered like she'd been waiting for my call.

"Tell me what your doctor tested."

I told her.

"Tell me the exact number."

I told her that too.

There was a long pause on the line. Long enough that I thought we'd dropped.

Then I heard her exhale.

"Honey. Your doctor checked the wrong test."

I pulled into a strip mall parking lot so I could write down what came next.

========

"What do you mean she checked the wrong test."

"Serum iron and ferritin are not the same thing.

"Serum iron is the iron floating in your blood right now.

"It changes hour to hour.

"You can eat a steak at lunch and your serum iron looks great by 3pm.

"Ferritin is your storage.

"It's the iron in your body's bank account.

"That's what your hair pulls from.

"Your hair doesn't care what's floating around in your blood today.

"Your hair cares what's in the vault.

"And almost every standard 'iron panel' your doctor orders... checks serum iron. Not ferritin."

I had to read what I'd just scribbled twice and then once more out loud to believe it.

Then I asked the obvious question.

"Is ferritin even on the regular blood test?"

"Sometimes. Not always.

"You have to ask for it specifically. By name. Spell it if you have to.

"And here's the part that's going to make you mad.

"Even when they do check ferritin, the lab cutoff for 'deficient' is 15 nanograms per milliliter. That's the number they flag.

"But women's hair researchers have been arguing since the 1990s that follicles need ferritin above 70 to function.

"Seventy.

"Not fifteen.

"So your ferritin can come back at 25, get reported as 'normal' on the lab sheet, and be functionally on the floor for hair purposes.

"That's a four-and-a-half-X gap between 'lab normal' and 'hair normal.'

"And nobody tells the women on these drugs that this is happening."

I sat in that parking lot for fifteen minutes.

========

I asked her how this happens to a body.

She let out a small laugh on her end of the line. I could hear her tapping a pen against something.

"Where do you want me to start."

"Start with the shot."

"OK. The shot does three things to your iron at the same time.

"One. Meat aversion. Almost every woman I talk to on these GLP-1s stops being able to look at red meat by month three. Some women can't even smell it. Heme iron, which is the only kind your body absorbs efficiently, comes from red meat. So her primary supply line just got cut.

"Two. You're eating 1,100 calories a day. Your body is in triage mode. It is shipping iron to your heart, your brain, your reproductive organs, your muscles. Your follicle is at the bottom of that list. Always.

"Three... and this is the one nobody talks about... your shot is putting you in metabolic stress.

"Rapid weight loss raises cortisol.

"Cortisol raises something called hepcidin.

"Hepcidin is the bouncer at the door of your gut.

"When hepcidin is high, it physically blocks the iron you do eat from absorbing.

"You can be swallowing a steak and an iron pill at the same time, and hepcidin will block more than half of it from ever entering your bloodstream.

"That's why your hair kept falling even after you started taking iron.

"You weren't absorbing what you were swallowing.

"And no doctor was going to catch it because they were measuring the wrong thing."

I had to put the car in park.

========

"OK," I said. "So I just need more iron."

"No."

She set something down. Maybe the pen.

"Three things have to happen at the same time.

"The cortisol has to come down. Or you can swallow iron until your tongue turns black and your ferritin will not move a single point.

"The co-factors have to be in place. Iron is the raw material. It can't get from your bloodstream into the follicle without copper. It can't be converted into the form your gut absorbs without Vitamin C. It can't be used to build a hair shaft without zinc. Most iron pills are just iron. Sitting there. With no tools.

"And then your follicle needs the structural protein it's been waiting eight months for.

"Keratin.

"Not biotin.

"Not collagen.

"Keratin peptides. The actual building block.

"Do those four things together and your storage starts to fill, the door at the gut opens, the iron moves where it needs to go, and your follicle has what it needs to make a hair shaft again."

I asked her how a person was supposed to do all of that.

She told me what her friend had told her.

========

It's called KeraLush.

It's the only women's hair supplement I have found that was actually designed for what happens to a woman's body on the shot.

Two capsules. Before bed.

It does not contain iron.

That is not what it is for.

What it does is hand the iron you're already eating, or already taking, the three tools it has been missing.

And it shuts down the cortisol that has been jamming the door at your gut closed for the last six months.

Here is what is in it. I will go slow.

I read this label four times in Renee's voice in my head before I ordered.

========

Vitamin C

The form that does one job perfectly.

It turns the iron in your food and your supplements from a form your body cannot absorb (Fe3+) into a form it can (Fe2+).

Without enough Vitamin C, the iron you eat walks straight through you.

This is why nutritionists tell you to squeeze lemon on your spinach.

Same biology. Higher dose.

========

Copper. 2 milligrams.

Renee explained this one twice.

Iron cannot get from your bloodstream into your follicle on its own.

It needs an escort protein called ceruloplasmin.

Ceruloplasmin needs copper to function.

No copper. No escort.

No escort. No delivery.

Most women eating 1,100 calories a day on the shot are running on empty for copper and don't know it.

So even if your ferritin started climbing tomorrow, your follicles would stay locked out of the supply line.

========

Zinc. 15 milligrams.

If iron is the raw material, zinc is what tells the follicle to start using it.

Without zinc the iron sits in the follicle unused, and your hair shaft never gets built no matter how full your storage gets.

========

Shoden® Ashwagandha.

This is the one that closes the loop.

Shoden is to ashwagandha what espresso is to decaf.

Drugstore ashwagandha is standardized to about 5 percent withanolides.

Shoden is standardized to 35 percent.

It is the most concentrated form of ashwagandha that exists on the market.

In a 60-day clinical trial it dropped cortisol 65.78 percent.

That number matters for one reason.

Cortisol is what is raising your hepcidin.

Hepcidin is the bouncer at the door of your gut.

When Shoden drops your cortisol, hepcidin drops with it.

And the door that has been blocking your iron absorption for the last six months... opens.

That is why every other hair supplement you have tried felt like it did nothing.

They were pushing the door from the outside while cortisol was holding it shut from the inside.

========

keraGEN-iV™ Keratin Peptides.

This is the structural material.

Your follicle has been sitting empty for eight months.

Even when the supply line reopens, it needs something to build with.

keraGEN-iV is a patented form of hydrolyzed keratin that is highly bioavailable.

The keratin in drugstore shampoos and conditioners is too large a molecule to absorb orally. keraGEN-iV is small enough to actually enter the bloodstream and reach the follicle.

In the published clinical study, women taking keraGEN-iV had a 43.1 percent reduction in hair pull score in 60 days.

What that means in normal language... if you were losing 200 strands a day, you would be down to about 114 by week 8.

Your shower drain stops looking like a crime scene.

Your pillow stops looking like you shared it.

========

I ordered three bottles on a Wednesday in October.

Two capsules before bed, every night, with a glass of water.

Pat Greene was supposed to direct the choir at our church's hundredth anniversary celebration in October.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Two news crews from Channel 11 and Channel 5.

Pat sat in the back pew of the church she has served for twenty-two years, behind the third pillar on the left side where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to her twenty-eight-year-old assistant Roxanne Holcomb conduct her choir.

Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

I'm going to say something most of us on these GLP-1 medications do not want to hear, and I'm not going to soften it because Pat did not get a soft version of this either.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

My name is Gloria Mason. I'm 67. I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. By June of last year I weighed two hundred and thirty-four — the most I had ever weighed in my life. My doctor told me my blood pressure was a hundred and sixty over a hundred and that we had two paths in front of us. I chose Ozempic®.

I started in July. By December I was down to one eighty-six. My pressure was normal. I had started walking on the trail at Stone Mountain Park three mornings a week. I had bought a dress at Phipps Plaza I had not had the courage to try on in twelve years.

I should have been thanking the Lord. The woman in the photograph on my dresser and the woman in my mirror were starting to match again.

Instead, I was sixty-seven years old, sitting in the back pew at Sunday morning service holding a folded handkerchief over my mouth because I had not gone normally in nine days and I could feel a sulphur burp coming up.

The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

I tried what he said. I tried what Sister Carolyn from the Mothers Board suggested. I tried what my daughter Tracey saw on TikTok. By August I had been to the bathroom five times in three weeks.

I am a retired guidance counselor. I track things. Between February and August I spent five hundred and twenty dollars on supplements and laxatives. Miralax morning and night. Citrucel at lunch. Metamucil at dinner. A magnesium from the GNC at Camp Creek. A probiotic my daughter Tracey ordered from Amazon for forty-eight dollars. A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Patricia Anne Greene and I have been friends since 1968. We were both twelve years old, both in Sister Mae Hudson's youth choir at Greater Mt. Zion, both not very good singers if I am being honest with you. Pat had a voice like clear water by the time she was sixteen. I had a voice that does not need to be discussed further. Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt. Zion for twenty-two years.

Our congregation does not have a Sunday service without Pat at that piano. Pat has not had a Sunday morning without our congregation since 1985. Marcus called her the heartbeat of our church right up until the day he passed.

She started Mounjaro® a year before I started Ozempic — same kind of grief story, different husband, hers passed in 2021. She lost fifty-one pounds. By December of '24 she was running again — she had been a sprinter at Spelman, I do not know if I told you that — and she was three months into rehearsals for the church's hundredth anniversary celebration scheduled for October. The committee had been planning it for two years. Pat was going to direct twelve special selections, a full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta, three guest soloists, and a praise dance from the youth ministry. Bishop Brown was coming from Washington. Two news crews.

In February she had a constipation streak that went fourteen days. She did not tell me. She did not tell her son Marcus Junior up in Athens. She filled out her own discontinuation paperwork on a Saturday night when she was alone in her kitchen. She quit her shots that week.

By May she had gained back twenty-three pounds. By July she had stopped coming to choir rehearsal — sent Roxanne in her place. By September she was up forty-six pounds. The depression came in heavy by the third week of September. She missed three Sundays in a row. People were calling me asking if Pat was all right. I did not know what to say.

The hundredth anniversary celebration was Sunday morning, October the twenty-first. The sanctuary was full. The Bishop preached for fifty-two minutes. Roxanne stood at Pat's piano and conducted Pat's program. Roxanne is twenty-eight years old. She is a very gifted young woman, the granddaughter of one of Pat's choir mothers from the eighties. She did her best.

Pat sat in the back pew on the left side, behind the third pillar where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to twenty-two years of her work being conducted by a young woman who had not yet been born when Pat first sat down at that piano.

After the service I went looking for her. Her car was already gone.

The next morning the church board met. By Wednesday word had spread that they were discussing transitioning Pat to "Music Minister Emeritus" — a respectful title for a forced retirement none of us thought we would see. Roxanne would take over permanently in January.

Wednesday evening women's Bible study, six-thirty to eight, the same group of women I have been studying scripture with for sixteen years. I had not been the last four Wednesdays. I had been telling myself I would skip another one and stay home in front of the television.

I do not skip Bible study. I made myself go.

There were six of us at the start of the cleanup. Most of the others had already gone home by the time I was folding the last three chairs.

Doreen Williams came back from the kitchen with a trash bag in her hand.

Doreen is seventy-two. She is one of the matriarchs of our church and a fellow Mothers Board member. She was the lead pharmacist at the Greene Brothers Pharmacy on Cascade Road in southwest Atlanta from 1981 until they closed in 2019 — thirty-eight years filling prescriptions for half the Black families on the southside of this city. She was Marcus's friend before she was mine. She and her husband John were at his funeral.

She set the trash bag down. She looked at me across the folding table.

"Gloria. Sister. You sit down. We need to talk before you drive yourself home."

I sat down.

I told her everything in about twelve minutes. The constipation. The burps in the receiving line. Pat. The discontinuation appointment Friday at one. I cried in the fellowship hall of the church Marcus and I had served for thirty-six years for the first time since the morning he passed.

Doreen handed me a clean napkin with the church's name printed at the corner from the stack on the table. Then she sat down across from me and folded her hands the way she used to do when she was about to explain to me what a new prescription would do to my husband's pressure.

"Sister Gloria. Can I tell you what I learned in thirty-eight years filling prescriptions at Greene Brothers?"

"Please."

This is what Mounjaro hair loss looks like.

Having a full mental breakdown under a helmet at 10pm.

I'm mad my ponytail is so thin I can't wear it without seeing scalp.

Mad at the garlic oil, the rosemary, the $40 biotin gummies that do nothing.

Mad that I can't even celebrate losing 40 lbs.

Now all I see in the mirror is how thin my hair's gotten.

I used to be the girl who had to thin out her ponytail because the elastic kept snapping.

The girl whose stylist sighed and said "we'll need an extra hour for the color, you have so much."

========

I started Tirz in March.

By August I'd lost 41 pounds.

I'd also lost what felt like half my hair.

The shower drain caught what looked like the tail of a small animal every week.

My pillow at 6am looked like I'd shared it with someone.

I emptied my brush three times getting ready, not once.

One week I put what came off the brush on my kitchen scale, because I couldn't tell anymore whether I was overreacting.

11 grams.

But I did the responsible thing.

I asked.

Sitting in her exam room, I said the words out loud.

"Could it be iron? My mom always had low iron. I haven't been able to eat red meat since I started the shot."

She ordered the test.

She called a week later.

"Your iron's great. It's just the shot. Hair grows back. Probably stress."

For two weeks I felt vindicated.

For three months I watched my hair keep falling.

========

Then I tried everything.

Biotin. Two bottles. $39.

The collagen everyone in the Facebook groups swears by. $94 a month for four months.

Minoxidil foam from the dermatologist after I begged for an appointment. $84.

Ferrous sulfate. Two bottles. $26. Constipated me for three months and my hair kept falling exactly the same way.

A red light therapy helmet. $800. Twenty minutes a night for three months, crying under it more than once.

Red light works on the surface. My problem was underneath it. I didn't know that yet.

Two rounds of PRP at my dermatologist's office. $1,100.

$2,425 in six months.

Zero hairs saved.

========

The friend who cracked it open was Liz.

She'd lost 30 pounds on Mounjaro the year before... and her hair.

In October she texted me at 8pm on a Wednesday.

Just a phone number.

"Call her. She's the one who fixed me."

Renee. Nurse practitioner. Hematology and women's health.

I called on my lunch break the next day.

"Tell me what your doctor tested."

I told her.

"Tell me the exact number."

I told her that too.

Long pause.

Then I heard her exhale.

"Honey. Your doctor checked the wrong test."

I pulled into a strip mall parking lot so I could write down what came next.

========

"Serum iron and ferritin are not the same thing.

Serum iron is what's floating in your blood right now. It changes hour to hour.

Ferritin is your body's iron bank account. That's what your hair pulls from.

Yours can read 25, get reported as normal, and be functionally empty for hair purposes.

And the shot does three things at once to drain it."

I sat in that parking lot for fifteen minutes.

========

Meat aversion. Most women on these can't look at red meat by month three. Heme iron, the only kind you absorb efficiently, comes from red meat. Supply line cut.

Hepcidin is the bouncer at the door of your gut.

When it's high, it physically blocks the iron you do eat from absorbing.

You can swallow a steak and an iron pill at the same time, and hepcidin will stop half of it from ever getting in.

That's why your hair kept falling after you started taking iron.

You weren't absorbing what you were swallowing.

And nobody was going to catch it, because they were measuring the wrong thing."

I put the car in park.

========

"So I need more iron."

"No."

She set the pen down.

"You need three things at the same time. The cortisol down, the co-factors in place, and the structural protein your follicle has been waiting eight months for.

Not biotin. Not collagen. Keratin.

And there isn't a single iron pill on the shelf that does any of that."

Pat Greene was supposed to direct the choir at our church's hundredth anniversary celebration in October.

She had been preparing the program for two years. Twelve special selections. A full orchestra brought in from Clark Atlanta. Three guest soloists, including the granddaughter of our founding pastor flown in from Houston. Eight hundred people in the sanctuary. The Bishop of the Sixth Episcopal District. Two news crews from Channel 11 and Channel 5.

Pat sat in the back pew of the church she has served for twenty-two years, behind the third pillar on the left side where she could not be seen from the pulpit, and listened to her twenty-eight-year-old assistant Roxanne Holcomb conduct her choir.

Pat had quit her Mounjaro® in February.

I'm going to say something most of us on these GLP-1 medications do not want to hear, and I'm not going to soften it because Pat did not get a soft version of this either.

Another bottle of fiber is not going to save your shots.

Not Miralax. Not Metamucil. Not the ninety-four-dollar prescription bulk-former your gastroenterologist called in last Thursday. Not the magnesium your daughter ordered for you off Amazon for forty-six dollars. Not the prune juice your mama swore by. Not the Smooth Move tea from the health food store in East Point.

NONE OF IT IS GOING TO WORK.

I know because I tried all of it for eleven months. And nine weeks ago I had a discontinuation appointment on the calendar for a Friday afternoon at one because I was done — done planning every Sunday morning around whether I could make it through service without leaving the sanctuary, done burping behind my hand at the Mothers Board meeting, done watching my own grandbabies and falling asleep on the couch while they watched cartoons at three in the afternoon.

I was going to walk into my prescriber's office at one o'clock, quit my Ozempic, and accept that I would be back to two hundred and thirty-four pounds within nine months. Maybe sooner. I had done it once before, after Marcus.

I almost let it happen. I was still listening to the same garbage that took my best friend's place at the piano.

Read every word of this. The answer is in here and it is not what your doctor told you.

My name is Gloria Mason. I'm 67. I live in Stone Mountain, Georgia — twenty minutes east of Atlanta — in the brick ranch house Marcus and I bought in 1989 with the down payment we saved for six years. Marcus passed eighteen months ago — September of '24, sudden heart attack at seventy-one, the morning after our forty-fifth anniversary dinner. He was retired from Aflac, he was a deacon at our church, and he was the only man I ever loved.

I have two grown daughters — Kendra in Tucker, Tracey in Decatur — and three grandchildren who keep me alive. I retired from Atlanta Public Schools in 2022 after thirty-two years as a guidance counselor, the last seventeen at Frederick Douglass High. I am active at Greater Mt. Zion AME Church, where Marcus and I were members for thirty-six years, and where I sit on the Mothers Board with eleven other women who have known me longer than my own daughters have.

In the nine months after Marcus passed, I ate. Not from hunger. From wanting something to do with my hands at seven in the morning when the house was too quiet. I gained fifty-six pounds. By June of last year I weighed two hundred and thirty-four — the most I had ever weighed in my life. My doctor told me my blood pressure was a hundred and sixty over a hundred and that we had two paths in front of us. I chose Ozempic®.

I started in July. By December I was down to one eighty-six. My pressure was normal. I had started walking on the trail at Stone Mountain Park three mornings a week. I had bought a dress at Phipps Plaza I had not had the courage to try on in twelve years.

I should have been thanking the Lord. The woman in the photograph on my dresser and the woman in my mirror were starting to match again.

Instead, I was sixty-seven years old, sitting in the back pew at Sunday morning service holding a folded handkerchief over my mouth because I had not gone normally in nine days and I could feel a sulphur burp coming up.

The constipation started in week four. By month three I was going every six or seven days, and only after a long fight. By month six the fight had stopped working.

The sulphur burps started in April. The kind that come up without warning. The kind that came up standing next to Pastor Womack on the receiving line after the eleven o'clock service. The kind I had never had in sixty-seven years of life. I started carrying breath mints in my pocketbook in a way I had not since I quit smoking in 1989.

The fatigue is what would have taken me. I am a sixty-seven-year-old woman with three grandbabies between two daughters who both work outside the home. I am the standing Tuesday and Thursday daycare. By July of last year I was driving to Kendra's house at two in the afternoon and falling asleep on the family-room couch while my eight-year-old grandson Caleb built Legos beside me on the floor. He told his mother. Kendra called me that night. She did not say it, but she was afraid.

And the brain fog. I lost the name of my own granddaughter Aniyah at the Mothers Board meeting in August. Just for fifteen seconds. I covered it. The two women across the table who noticed pretended they did not. I went out to my car in the church parking lot afterward and cried for ten minutes before I could drive home.

I told my prescriber.

"It happens with these medications, Mrs. Mason. Drink water. Try Miralax. Give it more time."

I tried what he said. I tried what Sister Carolyn from the Mothers Board suggested. I tried what my daughter Tracey saw on TikTok. By August I had been to the bathroom five times in three weeks.

I am a retired guidance counselor. I track things. Between February and August I spent five hundred and twenty dollars on supplements and laxatives. Miralax morning and night. Citrucel at lunch. Metamucil at dinner. A magnesium from the GNC at Camp Creek. A probiotic my daughter Tracey ordered from Amazon for forty-eight dollars. A prescription bulk-former my gastroenterologist wrote at ninety-four dollars out of pocket. Prune juice. Senna tea. A bottle of Smooth Move from a health-food store in East Point.

I had a basket of all of it in my pantry. Tracey saw it when she came over to drop off the grandbabies on a Sunday afternoon. She asked me what was happening. I told her I was fine.

I still had not gone normally in eight weeks. The sulphur burps were keeping me from communion on First Sundays. And meanwhile, my best friend Patricia was disappearing from the only thing she had ever loved more than us.

Patricia Anne Greene and I have been friends since 1968. We were both twelve years old, both in Sister Mae Hudson's youth choir at Greater Mt. Zion, both not very good singers if I am being honest with you. Pat had a voice like clear water by the time she was sixteen. I had a voice that does not need to be discussed further. Pat went on to study music education at Spelman College from '76 to '80, came back to our church in 1985, and was made music minister in 2003. She has been the music minister at Greater Mt.
